newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine trade deficit seen widening to $12 bln.
newsitem.headline: Philippine trade deficit seen widening to $12 bln.

text.p: The Philippines' eight-month trade deficit figure announced on Wednesday has led to expectations the gap for the full year could widen to between $12 billion and $12.5 billion, economists said.
"From a forecast of $11.5 billion, we've moved it up to $12 to $12.5 billion," Jose Mario Cuyegkeng, an economist at ING Barings Securities, said.
The trade deficit for January-August widened to $8.147 billion compared with $5.559 billion in the same period last year, the National Statistics Office reported on Wednesday.
"We were (earlier) looking at $10 billion for the whole year. The trade deficit will probably hit $12 billion," said Ernesto Pernia, a senior economist of the Asian Development Bank.
Imports rose by 26 percent to $21.197 billion from $16.766 billion during the first eight months, while exports rose by 16 percent to $13.051 billion from $11.207 billion.
Despite the expectations of a wider-than-expected deficit for the full year, economists said a drastic depreciation of the peso was not necessary.

The peso hit a year-low of 26.28 to the dollar last Monday, a mere 0.3 percent below the 26.20 at which it traded at the start of the year. By late on Wednesday, the peso had recovered to 26.265 to the dollar.
"There is no major reason for the peso to weaken. The trade deficit should not be a big factor for a major depreciation," said Rolando Valenzuela, senior vice- president of Philippine TA Securities.
Analysts said the wider trade deficit had been fuelled mostly by capital equipment imports and a slowdown in electronics exports in line with a worldwide trend.
But the trade gap had been funded by term financing as well as direct and portfolio investments, they said.
They said the country's balance of payments position, lower inflation rate and the interest rate premium of the peso all combined to limit any slide in the peso.
"The market just expects it (the peso) to hover around 26.30 pesos," ING Baring's Cuyegkeng said.
But to contain the trade deficit, "my preference is a slow depreciation rather than a sudden, drastic depreciation", he added.
He said a rapid depreciation could be a "double-edge sword". It would be favourable on the export side but would impact badly on inflation.
If the peso was allowed to weaken, "26.40 pesos is a worst-case scenario for me", said an economist who did not want to be named. "It can even be lower than 26.30 by year-end."
He added that if the peso dipped to 26.30 pesos, that would only be a 0.4 percentage point depreciation from the level the peso traded at the start of the year.
The movement would be minimal when compared to the six percentage points premium the peso enjoys over the dollar.
